title: Theory of Attachment and Place Attachment

findings.antecedent: Affective bond with places (home, neighborhood, city, country, continent)
findings.consequent: Positive effect on identity, meaning, values, goals, and significance
findings.quote: The feeling we experience towards certain places and to the communities that the places help to define and that are themselves defined by the places – home (family, relations, friends), workplace (colleagues), neighbourhood (neighbours), city, country, continent - certainly has a strong positive effect in defining our identity, in filling our life with meaning, in enriching it with values, goals and significance.

findings.antecedent: Equal attachment to the same place (by different groups)
findings.quote: These conflicts stem from an equal attachment to the same place, which puts them in competition.

findings.consequent: Spiritual unity for a scattered people
findings.quote: the importance in Jewish culture of the idea, or rather the feeling, of a 'Promised Land', of the greeting 'next year in Jerusalem' that kept a people, physically scattered to the four corners of the Earth, spiritually united for centuries.
it is perceived as one of those important factors that sometimes help and sometimes hinder our equilibrium, our material and spiritual well-being.

findings.antecedent: Early onset and stability of attachment cognitive structures
findings.consequent: Prototype of relational behavior, organizing principle of affective personality
findings.quote: the relationship of attachment thus comes to represent a prototype of relational behaviour, an organising principle (Stroufe and Waters, 1977) of the affective personality.

findings.antecedent: Richness of social interaction (intensity and quality)
findings.quote: The formation of an affective bond seems mainly to be a function of the richness of the social interaction (intensity and quality of the interaction) with the person(s) towards whom the attachment behaviour is directed

findings.antecedent: Stronger and healthier attachment to main figure
findings.quote: It seems even that the stronger and healthier the attachment to the main figure, the more likely there are to be secondary attachments (Bowlby, 1969, p. 308).

findings.consequent: Capacity to adapt internal working models to environment
findings.quote: The capacity to adapt the models to fit the environmental situation is greater in the case of healthy development, that is of secure attachment, whereas adaptation becomes more difficult in the case of insecure attachments, as defence mechanisms come into play (Bowlby, 1980).

findings.antecedent: Forced transfer from place of residence
findings.consequent: Sorrow, interruption of sense of continuity, fragmentation of spatial identity and group identity
findings.quote: the forced transfer from the place of residence represented an interruption in the individuals' sense of continuity, in that it involved the fragmentation of two essential components of identity, namely spatial identity and group identity, which are associated with strong affective elements.

findings.consequent: Feeling of belongingness, sorrow at moving out (age-linked)
findings.quote: length of residence seems to be closely linked both to the feeling of belongingness and to the sorrow at moving out of the community – both of which are also age-linked
interest in what goes on in the community decreases with age
Attachment to place is considered a fundamental human need (Relph, 1976)

findings.antecedent: Spatial uniformity, increased mobility, functionalistic relationship with places (contemporary society)
findings.consequent: Ability to satisfy attachment to place
findings.quote: contemporary society is increasingly unable to satisfy owing to its tendency towards gradual spatial uniformity, increased mobility and hence a purely functionalistic relationship with places.

findings.consequent: Universal and necessary for authentic relationship with environment
findings.quote: the geographers advance the hypothesis that the affective bonds in question are universal and necessary for an 'authentic' relationship with the environment.

findings.antecedent: Strong affective ties with place (for particular groups)
findings.quote: strong affective ties with the place of residence may be characteristic of particular groups of population under certain circumstances. Among other things, his work shows how such ties may to some extent prove dysfunctional, precluding adaptation to new opportunities (Fried 2000).

findings.antecedent: Congruity between needs and physical/social environmental resources
findings.quote: in positive cases attachment is developed, whereas in the case of incongruity, the individuals will either not form attachments or be repulsed.

findings.consequent: Individual hardship, conformist attitudes, social refutation
findings.quote: attachment does not necessarily have a positive outcome, but may represent a source of individual hardship, conformist attitudes or social refutation.

findings.antecedent: Positively-valenced knowledge of environment largely exceeds negatively-valenced knowledge
findings.consequent: Feeling of affection for a place
findings.quote: The feeling of affection for a place would develop in individuals whose positively-valenced knowledge of the environment in question largely exceeds the negatively-valenced knowledge.

findings.consequent: Feelings of affection or aversion for the place
findings.quote: places normally associated with a positive affect can also preclude the emergence of any feelings of affection or even cause aversion when they threaten the individual's identity.
a positive correlation between length of residence and the intensity of attachment to the place of residence is a widely reported finding

findings.consequent: Lack of affective bonds with places
findings.quote: the causal relationship postulated between high residential mobility and lack of affective bonds with places is far from having been proved.
attachment, that is the affective investment made in the neighbourhood of residence, is comparatively unaffected by the length of residence.

findings.antecedent: Modality of arrival in neighborhood (free vs. compulsory choice)
findings.quote: the modality of arrival in the neighbourhood, or the perception of whether it was a free or a compulsory choice, carries greater weight.

findings.antecedent: High degree of mobility during childhood
findings.quote: a high degree of mobility during childhood is associated with a greater desire for stability in adulthood

findings.antecedent: Neighborhood quality, previous experiences, compatibility with residential identity
findings.quote: Affective investment seems to be closely linked to neighbourhood quality, but also to previous experiences and compatibility with residential identity.

findings.antecedent: Environments experienced in childhood or adolescence
findings.quote: Strong positive affective bonds seem to develop towards the environments experienced in childhood or adolescence, and more occasionally towards environments experienced only in adulthood.

findings.antecedent: Unsatisfactory residential experiences during infancy and adolescence
findings.consequent: Capacity to form attachments in adulthood
findings.quote: unsatisfactory residential experiences occurring during infancy and adolescence seem to have negative long-term consequences on the capacity to form attachments in adulthood, even towards the more satisfactory environments.

findings.consequent: Expression of individual/social identity, strength of attachment
findings.quote: primary territories are better able to express individual identity and are characterised by stronger feelings of attachment, while secondary territories tend to express a social or group identity.
the street layout can facilitate attachment to the neighbourhood and thus the development of a secondary territoriality.
the 'tendency to equate attachment with more permanent residences may have more to do with our cultural bias toward home ownership than with reality' (p. 297).

findings.antecedent: Prolonged association between individual and place
findings.quote: prolonged association between an individual and a place is widely recognised as one of the distinctive features of attachment to place.
individuals may not be conscious of their attachment to a place... and only become aware of it under particular circumstances, such as when the bond is threatened.

findings.consequent: Place of greatest affection for majority (but few want to return)
findings.quote: for the vast majority the place of greatest affection is one's birthplace, but there is also a great variability related to mobility experiences and life stages.

findings.antecedent: Age of moving away from birthplace (after 12 vs. earlier)
findings.consequent: Strength and nature of birthplace bond (strong nostalgic bond for later movers vs. only warm memories for earlier movers)
findings.quote: among people who had moved away after the age of 12, there were strong bonds to the birthplace in a 'nostalgic' sense, as there was no intention to move back. Among those who had moved away at an earlier age, 'only some warm memories for the former place remained'.
bonds with sacred places discussed by Mazumdar and Mazumdar (1993) are very intense.

findings.antecedent: Involuntary separation from place or loss of place
findings.consequent: Distress, grief (similar to loss of loved one)
findings.quote: The fact that reactions similar to those for the loss of a loved one can be felt in relation to places was the starting point for the considerations on attachment to places

findings.consequent: Symptoms of malaise (mixed relationship with health)
findings.quote: a high index of mobility is associated with an increased presence of symptoms of malaise, but also that the relationship between mobility and health is not always negative.

findings.antecedent: Less opportunity for choice (obliged to live in unsatisfactory environment)
findings.quote: Persons with less opportunity for choice who are obliged to live in an environment that does not come up to their expectations are more likely to have health problems than those with a high residential mobility.

findings.consequent: Future mobility (as a strategy to correct undesirable aspects)
findings.quote: mobility may be a strategy to correct undesirable aspects of one's life and one such undesirable aspect could be lack of attachment, since such a lack is a significant indicator of future mobility.

findings.consequent: Feeling of security for young children (not physical protection)
findings.quote: the feeling of security is perceived as particularly important by the younger children (less than 13 years old) and is not a function of the physical protection offered by the home but of permanence (in Bowlbian terms we could say of accessibility).
the feeling of comfort appears more and more frequently in women's description of homes.

findings.antecedent: Life stage (childhood, old age vs. adolescence, adulthood)
findings.quote: the need for security and protection preponderates during certain stages of life (e.g. childhood and old age), while other needs emerge more forcefully in adolescence and at various stages of adult life (e.g. exploration, affiliation, self-expression, etc.).

findings.consequent: Strong attachment to home (interpreted as re-emergence of security/protection need)
findings.quote: The strong attachment the elderly display towards the home might thus be seen as the re-emergence of the dominant need for security and protection.

findings.antecedent: Impaired physical resources, diminished capacity to adapt spatial behavior (elderly)
findings.quote: Impaired physical resources and the diminished capacity to adapt spatial behaviour patterns to changes in the immediate environment contribute to making the elderly retreat from the novel and seek security.

the stronger attachment to the neighbourhood found among the lower classes might be accounted for by the continued activation of stress reducing behaviours connected with poverty of resources (Fried 2000).
